desc:
Each meeting is a half-open time range [start, end): it occupies every moment t with start ≤ t < end. A meeting that ends at time 10 and one that starts at time 10 do not clash.

You are a single person and cannot be in two meetings at the same moment. Given all the meetings (in no particular order), return true if you can attend every one of them, and false otherwise.

meetings = [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]  ->  false
meetings = [[7, 10], [2, 4]]            ->  true
hints: Two meetings clash exactly when each one starts before the other one ends. Comparing every pair works, but it is O(n<sup>2</sup>).
If the meetings were listed by start time, which pairs would you actually have to look at?
Sort by start time. Then a clash exists if and only if some meeting starts before the previous meeting in sorted order has ended.
editorial: Sort the meetings by start time. Suppose two meetings clash, and let them be at positions i < j in sorted order. Then start[j] < end[i]. The meeting right after i has a start no later than start[j], so it also starts before end[i]; hence it is enough to compare each meeting with its neighbour.

Scan the sorted list and return false as soon as start[i] < end[i-1]. Using a strict comparison makes back-to-back meetings legal. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, and O(n) space for the sorted copy.
